case: Our food delivery app takes about 2,000 orders a minute at lunch peak. The order service is written in Python, uses PostgreSQL on AWS and calls an external payment provider. Last month, app retries during a slow payment period created duplicated orders and double charges. In the first months, this person will own the order placement flow and get it ready for twice today's peak.

questions.q: An index made our order lookup fast, but inserts slowed down at peak. Explain why, and how you'd decide which indexes to keep.
questions.deep: How would you see this in PostgreSQL?
questions.expect: Write cost of each index, bloat, read vs write ratio; uses query stats and EXPLAIN to decide with data.

questions.q: Two requests update the same order at the same time. What can go wrong, and how do transaction isolation levels help?
questions.deep: When would you lock the row instead of raising the isolation level?
questions.expect: Lost updates and anomalies per level; row locking vs optimistic locking with a version column.

questions.q: What does it mean for an endpoint to be idempotent, and how would you make POST /orders idempotent?
questions.deep: Where do you store the idempotency key, and for how long?
questions.expect: Client key, unique constraint, stored response, TTL; handles two identical requests arriving at once.

questions.q: When would you process something with a queue instead of inside the request, and what do you give up?
questions.deep: How do you avoid losing a message if the service crashes right after writing to the database?
questions.expect: Latency and decoupling vs consistency and complexity; at-least-once delivery, outbox pattern, deduplication.

questions.q: p95 latency of POST /orders went from 200 ms to 2 s at lunch and the database CPU is at 90%. Walk me through it.
questions.deep: What would make you change your first hypothesis?
questions.expect: Method: metrics, slow queries, locks, connections; narrows down with data; mitigates before the root cause.

questions.q: Tell me about the hardest production bug you've chased. How did you find it?
questions.deep: What did you try first that didn't work?
questions.expect: Real case, hypotheses tested with data, reproduced it, verified the fix and added a test or an alert.

questions.q: We see duplicated orders a few times a day. How would you find where they come from?
questions.deep: How would you prove your fix worked?
questions.expect: Correlates request IDs and logs, looks for retries and races, checks constraints; measures duplicates after.

questions.q: Tell me about a time a deploy of yours broke production. What did you do, and what changed after?
questions.deep: How long until customers stopped being affected?
questions.expect: Fast rollback, clear communication, blameless follow-up with concrete prevention (tests, canary, flags).

questions.q: Design the order placement flow for 2,000 orders a minute at peak, so a retry from the app or a slow payment provider never creates a duplicate order or a double charge. Draw it end to end.
questions.deep: Walk me through what happens if the payment provider times out after charging.
questions.expect: Idempotency keys, order state machine, outbox or queue, reconciliation with the provider; covers each failure path.

questions.q: How would you model the orders and payments tables for your design?
questions.deep: Which database constraints protect you even if the code has a bug?
questions.expect: Clear states, unique keys for idempotency and provider IDs, foreign keys, audit trail; money stays consistent.

questions.q: In your design, what happens when the payment provider is down for 10 minutes at peak?
questions.deep: What does the customer see in the app?
questions.expect: Timeouts, circuit breaker, pending state or queue, clear message to the user, retry and reconcile later.

questions.q: If you had half the time to ship, what would you cut from your design, and what would you never cut?
questions.deep: What risk are you accepting with that cut?
questions.expect: Keeps idempotency and money consistency; defers nice-to-haves; names the accepted risk explicitly.

questions.q: Traffic doubles next year. What breaks first in your design, and how would you know before it does?
questions.deep: Which load test would you run, and what result means we're ready?
questions.expect: Finds the bottleneck (writes, connections), load tests with a clear threshold, metrics and alerts, scaling steps.

questions.q: How would you scale PostgreSQL writes for orders without losing consistency?
questions.deep: When would you split the database, and what would it cost?
questions.expect: Connection pooling, query tuning, partitioning, replicas for reads; sharding only with a clear need and its costs.

questions.q: Which security risks worry you most in an order and payment API, and how would you handle them?
questions.deep: How do you keep card data out of your systems?
questions.expect: AuthN and AuthZ, validation, rate limiting, secrets, tokens from the provider instead of card data, audit logs.

questions.q: Which metrics and alerts would you put on the order flow to catch problems before customers do?
questions.deep: Which one would wake you up at night?
questions.expect: Order and payment success rate, latency, duplicates, queue age; alerts on customer impact, not CPU.

questions.q: Tell me about a technical decision of yours that saved or cost the business money. How do you know?
questions.deep: What number did you or someone else measure?
questions.expect: Real decision, impact in money, customers or time with a number, and what they learned.

questions.q: Product wants a new promotions feature next month, but you want to fix the duplicated orders first. How do you make the case?
questions.deep: What would you accept as a compromise?
questions.expect: Explains the cost of duplicates (refunds, support, trust), proposes sequencing or scope, decides together.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you explained a technical trade-off to someone non-technical. How did it go?
questions.deep: How did you know they understood?
questions.expect: Plain words, focus on impact and options, checks understanding; a real outcome.

questions.q: How would you explain the duplicated orders to the support team in two sentences?
questions.deep: What would you ask them to tell customers?
questions.expect: Plain words: what happened, who's affected, what's being done and when. No jargon, no blame.
